autort-embodied-foundation-models-for-la.tldr: Uses an LLM to propose diverse tasks filtered by safety, enabling large-scale real-world robot data collection in offices.
autort-embodied-foundation-models-for-la.whatChanged: Before AutoRT, robot data collection required hand-scripting each task or narrow teleoperation, limiting diversity and scale. This paper showed that an LLM could autonomously propose varied, safe tasks for fleets of mobile manipulators, collecting thousands of demonstrations with minimal human oversight.
autort-embodied-foundation-models-for-la.soWhat: AutoRT lets robots decide what to practice on their own, like a coach giving a team of athletes different drills chosen by a smart assistant that also checks no one gets hurt. This means robots can learn many new skills from real-world experience without a person having to program every single move.
autort-embodied-foundation-models-for-la.industry: AutoRT established the fleet-scale, LLM-directed data collection loop now used by several robotics companies to gather diverse real-world demonstrations without manual task scripting. Its safety filtering pattern has been adopted in subsequent autonomy stacks, reducing deployment risk in semi-structured environments like offices and warehouses.
autort-embodied-foundation-models-for-la.graphicPrompt: A fleet of three wheeled robot arms in an office hallway, each reaching toward different objects (a cup, a book, a stapler). Above them, a glowing brain icon connected by dashed lines to each robot. Between the brain and robots, a translucent shield icon filters the task descriptions.

rt-1-robotics-transformer-for-real-world.tldr: A transformer policy trained on 130k robot episodes maps images and language to discretized actions for hundreds of tasks.
rt-1-robotics-transformer-for-real-world.whatChanged: Before RT-1, robot control often required separate models or hand-tuned controllers for each task, limiting scalability. This paper showed that a single transformer trained on diverse real-world demonstrations can generalize across hundreds of manipulation tasks at practical control rates, replacing per-task pipelines.
rt-1-robotics-transformer-for-real-world.soWhat: Think of it like a universal remote that works for every appliance instead of needing a different remote for each one. Before, robots needed a separate program for every chore; now one model can handle many different instructions by learning from lots of examples.
rt-1-robotics-transformer-for-real-world.industry: RT-1 established the transformer architecture as the standard backbone for generalist robot policies, directly influencing follow-up systems like RT-2 and Open X-Embodiment. It enabled Google DeepMind and others to move toward unified deployment on real hardware, reducing the engineering cost of reprogramming for each new task.
rt-1-robotics-transformer-for-real-world.graphicPrompt: A robotic arm over a table with three distinct objects: a red cube, a blue cup, and a yellow sponge. Dashed lines from the gripper trace three different trajectories toward each object, with a camera icon above the arm. No text, letters, logos, or faces.

robocat-a-self-improving-foundation-agen.tldr: A generalist agent that adapts to new robotic tasks from ~100 demos and self-improves by generating its own practice data.
robocat-a-self-improving-foundation-agen.whatChanged: Before RoboCat, robot learning typically required large datasets or manual data collection per task, and models rarely improved autonomously. This paper showed that a single agent can adapt to novel tasks and robot embodiments with very few demonstrations, then generate its own training data through self-practice, compounding its skills across successive tasks.
robocat-a-self-improving-foundation-agen.soWhat: RoboCat learns a new job after watching it done just 100 times, then practices on its own to get better, just like a musician who learns a new song from sheet music and then improves through repeated play.
robocat-a-self-improving-foundation-agen.industry: This paper validated that self-generated data can drive rapid skill acquisition, enabling robot teams to cut the cost of adding a new task by allowing the model to train itself. It laid groundwork for autonomous data loops used in foundation models for robotics, and its approach influences how DeepMind and others now build generalist manipulation agents that improve in deployment.
robocat-a-self-improving-foundation-agen.graphicPrompt: A single robot arm reaches toward a table holding a blue block and a red mug. Above the arm, a circular arrow loops from the gripper back to a small icon of a brain or gears, symbolizing self-generated practice data. No text or logos.

rt-2-vision-language-action-models-trans.tldr: Co-fine-tunes a web-scale vision-language model on robot trajectories so the resulting vision-language-action model inherits internet knowledge and generalizes to unseen objects and instructions.
rt-2-vision-language-action-models-trans.whatChanged: Before RT-2, robotic control models typically required task-specific data or simulation, limiting their ability to handle novel objects or instructions. This paper showed that a web-scale vision-language model, when co-fine-tuned on robot trajectory data, transfers broad semantic and visual knowledge to physical control, enabling zero-shot generalization to unseen objects and commands without additional training data.
rt-2-vision-language-action-models-trans.soWhat: Imagine a robot that only knew how to pick up objects it had seen before; RT-2 is like giving that robot access to all the pictures and descriptions on the internet, so it can handle new objects just by recognizing them from web images. It turns a large internet-trained image recognition system into a robot controller that can act on vague instructions like 'pick up the apple' even if it never saw that specific apple in a robot demo.
rt-2-vision-language-action-models-trans.industry: RT-2 proved that web pretraining transfers directly to physical control, establishing the default architecture for commercial robot foundation models—nearly all such models now start from a pretrained vision-language model. This paradigm reduces the need for massive robot-specific data collection and enables companies like Google DeepMind to deploy generalist robots that can handle diverse tasks in unstructured environments.
rt-2-vision-language-action-models-trans.graphicPrompt: A robotic arm on a table reaches toward a banana, a pencil, a cup, and a toy car. Above the arm, a large cloud shape contains abstract icons (a globe, a book, a gear) representing web pretraining. The arm's gripper is positioned to grasp the banana, which is slightly separated from other objects to emphasize unseen-object generalization. No text, letters, logos, or faces.

open-x-embodiment-robotic-learning-datas.tldr: Aggregates 1M+ trajectories from 22 robots; cross-embodiment RT-X policies achieve positive transfer.
open-x-embodiment-robotic-learning-datas.whatChanged: Before, robotic learning datasets were mostly single-robot or limited in diversity. This paper released a multi-robot dataset spanning 22 embodiments and showed that training a single RT-X model across all robots improves policy performance, enabling positive transfer between different robot morphologies.
open-x-embodiment-robotic-learning-datas.soWhat: Think of it as a shared school library where each robot donates its own homework problems and solutions; now every robot can study from everyone else's work. This lets a robot learn a task it never saw before by drawing on experience from a completely different robot type.
open-x-embodiment-robotic-learning-datas.industry: This paper contributed the Open X-Embodiment dataset as a public benchmark and the RT-X model family as pre-trained starting points. Industry teams now use this corpus to bootstrap robot policies, evaluate cross-embodiment transfer, and inform data collection strategies across heterogeneous fleets.
open-x-embodiment-robotic-learning-datas.graphicPrompt: A large worktable holds 22 differently shaped robot arms and grippers reaching toward a central pile of assorted objects. Glowing lines connect each robot to a single server rack labeled 'RT-X' in the background. No text, no faces.

do-as-i-can-not-as-i-say-grounding-langu.tldr: Grounds large language model plans in robot affordances, so robot executes only feasible steps and replans upon failure.
do-as-i-can-not-as-i-say-grounding-langu.whatChanged: Before SayCan, large language models could propose high-level plans but had no way to verify if steps were physically possible for a given robot. This paper introduced a system where the LLM proposes candidate actions and a learned affordance model scores each action's feasibility, so the robot only executes actions it can actually perform and re-plans when a step fails.
do-as-i-can-not-as-i-say-grounding-langu.soWhat: Imagine a cook who hears a recipe but only follows steps they have the ingredients and tools for, skipping or adjusting the rest. This lets robots follow natural-language instructions safely by ignoring commands they can't physically carry out.
do-as-i-can-not-as-i-say-grounding-langu.industry: The paper established the 'LLM reasons, robot filters' pattern now used in industrial and service robotics to turn language commands into executable action sequences. Google and other labs have since integrated similar affordance-filtering loops into pick-and-place, assembly, and mobile manipulation systems.
do-as-i-can-not-as-i-say-grounding-langu.graphicPrompt: A robotic arm over a table with a block and a cup. Above the arm, a speech bubble from a language model lists steps like 'pick block', 'pour cup', 'move left'. Two steps have red X marks; the arm reaches for the block. No text or faces.

pi0-a-vision-language-action-flow-model-.tldr: A 3B-parameter vision-language-action model using flow-matching for dexterous multi-robot control, fine-tuned from a pretrained VLM.
pi0-a-vision-language-action-flow-model-.whatChanged: Before this paper, robot control models were often task-specific or limited in dexterity. This paper shows that a single model can be fine-tuned for diverse dexterous tasks across multiple robot platforms by combining a pretrained VLM with flow-matching action generation. It made possible a generalist robot brain that can be adapted to new hardware and tasks with minimal additional data.
pi0-a-vision-language-action-flow-model-.soWhat: Imagine a robot brain that can learn many different skills from watching videos of humans, like folding laundry or clearing a table. This paper shows how to make such a brain by combining a language-understanding model with a new way to generate smooth, precise robot movements.
pi0-a-vision-language-action-flow-model-.industry: The paper contributed a licensable generalist robot brain (π0) that companies can adapt to their own hardware and task suites. It introduced flow-matching action generation, which enables more fluid and precise manipulation. Physical Intelligence offers π0 for licensing, and other companies are using it to accelerate development of dexterous robot applications.
pi0-a-vision-language-action-flow-model-.graphicPrompt: A robot arm with a gripper folding a towel on a table, while a digital brain icon hovers above, connected by flowing lines. In the background, a pretrained VLM network morphs into the action model. No text or faces.

fast-efficient-robot-action-tokenization.tldr: FAST tokenizes continuous robot actions into discrete tokens using frequency-domain compression, enabling efficient autoregressive training of vision-language-action models.
fast-efficient-robot-action-tokenization.whatChanged: Before FAST, tokenizing continuous robot actions required high-resolution discretization or special architectures, leading to slow training and high cost. FAST introduces a frequency-domain tokenizer that compresses action chunks into a compact discrete sequence, allowing vision-language-action models to be trained autoregressively at much higher speed and lower cost without losing dexterity.
fast-efficient-robot-action-tokenization.soWhat: Imagine trying to write down every tiny movement of a robot arm in a language the robot understands. FAST turns those movements into a short code using a trick similar to how JPEG compresses pictures, so the robot can learn much faster and cheaper.
fast-efficient-robot-action-tokenization.industry: This paper contributed a practical tokenization method that reduces vision-language-action model training time and cost by roughly an order of magnitude, making fast action tokenization a standard ingredient in commercial robot models from Physical Intelligence. It enables deployment of more capable robot control policies with less computational resources.
fast-efficient-robot-action-tokenization.graphicPrompt: A robot arm holds a cube, its trajectory shown as a wavy line. A magnifying glass reveals the line transformed into a neat stack of colored blocks, like a musical scale, indicating compression of continuous motion into discrete tokens.

teaching-robots-to-listen-and-think-hard.tldr: Two-level system: VLM breaks complex prompts into single steps for π0 low-level policy, trained on synthetic interactions.
teaching-robots-to-listen-and-think-hard.whatChanged: Before, robots could not handle multi-stage requests or mid-task corrections interactively. This paper introduced a hierarchical architecture where a VLM acts as a high-level planner that decomposes natural language commands into simple sub-tasks for a low-level policy, enabling real-time corrections and robust execution.
teaching-robots-to-listen-and-think-hard.soWhat: Imagine a robot assistant that listens to a complicated instruction like 'set the table and then pour coffee'—a smart manager inside the robot splits it into easy steps the robot can do one at a time. If you interrupt mid-task to say 'use the red cup instead', the manager adjusts the plan on the fly.
teaching-robots-to-listen-and-think-hard.industry: This paper contributed a concrete architecture and synthetic data pipeline for training conversational robot assistants that can follow multi-stage instructions and accept live corrections. The interaction model is now deployed in service and retail robots, enabling them to handle complex requests from customers.
teaching-robots-to-listen-and-think-hard.graphicPrompt: A robot arm reaching toward a cup on a table. Above the robot, a thought bubble shows two sequential icons: a cup and then a door. A human hand points to a different cup on the table, and the thought bubble changes to show that cup icon followed by the door. The scene is simple shapes and no text.

vlas-that-train-fast-run-fast-and-genera.tldr: Knowledge insulation stops action expert gradients from overwriting the VLM backbone, enabling fast training and strong generalization.
vlas-that-train-fast-run-fast-and-genera.whatChanged: Before this paper, adding continuous action experts to a VLM often caused backward gradient interference that slowed training or eroded web-scale semantic knowledge. Knowledge insulation isolates these gradients, so the model trains as fast as tokenized VLAs while preserving language understanding and improving zero-shot generalization.
vlas-that-train-fast-run-fast-and-genera.soWhat: Imagine a chef who learns a new recipe without forgetting old techniques because the new instructions are kept in a separate notebook. This method lets robot models learn new physical skills quickly without losing the language and common sense they learned from the internet.
vlas-that-train-fast-run-fast-and-genera.industry: This work directly improves the training speed and deployment reliability of robot manipulation models, cutting compute cost and boosting language following in unseen environments. Physical Intelligence integrates it into their own VLA pipeline, and the technique can be adopted by any team building visuomotor policies on top of pretrained vision-language models.
vlas-that-train-fast-run-fast-and-genera.graphicPrompt: A robot arm reaches for a block on a table. Beside the arm, a large glowing brain icon (VLM) is connected by a thin insulated wire to a smaller gear icon (action expert). A lightning bolt gradient flows from the gear but is stopped by a zigzag insulator barrier before reaching the brain.

emergence-of-human-to-robot-transfer-in-.tldr: Co-fine-tuning a scaled VLA on egocentric human video transfers to robot behavior, with emergence as robot data grows, improving 2x where scarce.
emergence-of-human-to-robot-transfer-in-.whatChanged: Before this paper, it was unclear whether human egocentric video alone could transfer to robot behavior in large VLAs, and robot data was expensive. This paper shows that simply co-fine-tuning on human video yields robot behavior, and that this transfer ability emerges as the amount of robot pretraining data increases. It makes cheap human video a viable source for improving robot skills, especially in data-scarce scenarios.
emergence-of-human-to-robot-transfer-in-.soWhat: Imagine teaching a robot to cook by letting it watch you through a head-mounted camera. This paper shows the robot can learn from those videos, especially if it already knows other tasks from expensive demonstrations, so you can teach new tasks with cheap human videos.
emergence-of-human-to-robot-transfer-in-.industry: This paper introduces a practical method to use cheap, wearable human video data to train robot VLAs, drastically cutting the required amount of expensive robot teleoperation data for new tasks. It enables faster scaling of robot deployment across diverse tasks by leveraging a widely available data source. Physical Intelligence can incorporate this into their VLA models to reduce data collection costs for real-world applications.
emergence-of-human-to-robot-transfer-in-.graphicPrompt: A head-mounted camera on a human shows an egocentric view of hands assembling a shelf. Next to the human, a robot arm mimics the hand movements. An arrow from camera to computer screen, then to robot, indicates data flow. No text, faces, or logos.

vlas-with-long-and-short-term-memory.tldr: Multi-scale memory stores video clips and language summaries, enabling robots to complete 15-minute tasks and recover from errors.
vlas-with-long-and-short-term-memory.whatChanged: Before this paper, robot policies with VLAs were limited to short tasks because they lacked persistent memory across time. This paper introduces a memory system that stores short-horizon video frames and long-horizon language summaries, allowing tasks up to 15 minutes long and in-context recovery from earlier mistakes.
vlas-with-long-and-short-term-memory.soWhat: Think of a robot with a notepad where it quickly sketches what it sees every few seconds and writes a longer diary entry every few minutes, so it can remember the whole cooking session. This means a robot can prepare a full meal without needing to start over if it drops a spoon.
vlas-with-long-and-short-term-memory.industry: This work introduces a practical memory architecture for VLA-based robot policies, enabling long-duration tasks (15 minutes) in commercial cleaning, service, and kitchen settings. It reduces the need for human resets and supervision, moving robots closer to viable deployment in messy, real-world environments.
vlas-with-long-and-short-term-memory.graphicPrompt: A robot arm in a kitchen placing a pot on a stove. To the left, a floating screen showing a rapid sequence of video frames from the last 30 seconds. To the right, a floating notepad with bullet-point text summaries of earlier steps. No text, no letters, no human faces.

precise-manipulation-with-efficient-onli.tldr: RL tokens compress VLA state for a tiny on-robot actor-critic, enabling fast online learning that speeds precise manipulation up to 3x from 15 minutes of data.
precise-manipulation-with-efficient-onli.whatChanged: Prior methods for fine-tuning dexterous manipulation required off-robot retraining or large amounts of online data. This paper introduces RL tokens, a compact representation of the vision-language-action model's internal state, allowing an efficient actor-critic to learn online directly on the robot and accelerate the most precise phases of tasks threefold with only about 15 minutes of real-world interaction.
precise-manipulation-with-efficient-onli.soWhat: Imagine a chef who can instantly tweak a recipe mid-cook instead of sending the dish back to the test kitchen. The robot uses a short practice session to learn millimeter-accurate adjustments on the spot, making it practical for real-world deployment where every factory line or job site is slightly different.
precise-manipulation-with-efficient-onli.industry: Physical Intelligence’s approach enables deployed robots to improve their own precision tasks without being returned to a research lab, reducing downtime and increasing autonomy. This is immediately relevant for manufacturing, assembly, and construction robots that must adapt to part tolerances or environmental variation on the line.
precise-manipulation-with-efficient-onli.graphicPrompt: A robotic arm reaching toward a peg-in-hole assembly; a small glowing cube labeled 'RL token' floats inside the arm's base. A nearby speedometer needle points to '3x' and a clock icon shows '15 min'. No text, letters, or faces.

real-time-action-chunking-with-large-mod.tldr: Real-time action chunking for diffusion-based VLAs generates next chunk while previous executes, eliminating discontinuities without training changes.
real-time-action-chunking-with-large-mod.whatChanged: Previously, using large vision-language-action models for real-time control required either waiting for full inference before acting, causing latency, or using naive smoothing that introduced discontinuities. This paper introduces a method to generate the next action chunk concurrently with executing the previous one, maintaining smooth transitions without any modifications during training.
real-time-action-chunking-with-large-mod.soWhat: Think of a factory robot that needs to decide its next move while still finishing the current one. This paper lets the robot plan ahead in real-time without jerky pauses, like a chef chopping vegetables while already deciding which pan to reach for next.
real-time-action-chunking-with-large-mod.industry: This technique enables deployment of large VLAs on robots with reasonable latency (100-300 ms), making it practical for industrial settings where cycle times matter. Physical Intelligence likely integrates this into their generalist robot models to allow faster, smoother operation without retraining. It could be used by robotics companies needing real-time action generation with high-capacity models.
real-time-action-chunking-with-large-mod.graphicPrompt: A robot arm holding a component in mid-air, with a ghostly transparent arm showing the next planned grasp. Above the arm, a streaming timeline: one chunk finishing, next chunk starting without gap. No text, no logos, no faces.

nvidia-isaac-sim-enabling-scalable-gpu-a.tldr: Independent survey reviews Isaac Sim's architecture, compares with other simulators across five robotics domains, and analyses practical limits.
nvidia-isaac-sim-enabling-scalable-gpu-a.whatChanged: Before this paper, GPU-accelerated simulation comparisons were often vendor-driven or anecdotal. This paper provides an independent, structured evaluation that maps where Isaac Sim outperforms alternatives and where its limitations lie, enabling evidence-based simulator selection.
nvidia-isaac-sim-enabling-scalable-gpu-a.soWhat: Think of it like a car review that tests different vehicles on highway vs. city driving. This paper tests Isaac Sim against other robot simulators across five different tasks, so engineers know which simulator saves time and gives accurate results for their specific robot project.
nvidia-isaac-sim-enabling-scalable-gpu-a.industry: The paper gives robotics engineering teams a clear decision framework for choosing simulation tools, reducing guesswork and hardware investment risk. It is used by product teams to optimize simulation pipelines for manipulation, navigation, and other domains, shortening development cycles.
nvidia-isaac-sim-enabling-scalable-gpu-a.graphicPrompt: A side-by-side comparison grid: five columns each labeled with an icon (e.g., robotic arm, drone, warehouse robot). Rows show speed (stopwatch) and fidelity (magnifying glass) bars for Isaac Sim and three other simulators. No text, only icons and color-coded bars.

isaac-lab-a-gpu-accelerated-simulation-f.tldr: NVIDIA’s successor to Isaac Gym provides a single composable GPU-accelerated framework for physics, rendering, and sensor simulation for robot learning.
isaac-lab-a-gpu-accelerated-simulation-f.whatChanged: Previous robot simulators often required separate pipelines for physics, rendering, and sensor modeling, limiting parallelism and speed. Isaac Lab unifies these on a single GPU kernel, enabling thousands of parallel environments and reducing training time from weeks to hours.
isaac-lab-a-gpu-accelerated-simulation-f.soWhat: Training a robot to walk or grasp used to take days or weeks of computer time because only one or a few simulations could run at once. Isaac Lab lets a single GPU run thousands of simulated robots simultaneously, so training happens in hours.
isaac-lab-a-gpu-accelerated-simulation-f.industry: Isaac Lab has become the standard training substrate for NVIDIA's robot learning research and is used by robotics teams for whole-body, locomotion, and dexterous policy development. It directly feeds into deployments via NVIDIA's Isaac Sim and Omniverse platforms.
isaac-lab-a-gpu-accelerated-simulation-f.graphicPrompt: A large rectangular GPU chip at the center, with glowing threads connecting to dozens of small robot avatars in different virtual environments: a legged robot on rocky ground, a robot arm assembling blocks, a drone hovering over a grid. Robots are semi-transparent wireframe to indicate simulation. No text or logos.

a-careful-examination-of-large-behavior-.tldr: Extends Diffusion Policy into Large Behavior Models for multitask dexterous manipulation, finding multitask pretraining improves success, robustness, and data efficiency.
a-careful-examination-of-large-behavior-.whatChanged: Before this paper, Diffusion Policy was primarily a single-task model. This paper scales it to a multitask 'Large Behavior Model', showing through blinded randomized trials that multitask pretraining improves success rates and robustness while requiring less data per task.
a-careful-examination-of-large-behavior-.soWhat: Imagine teaching a chef many recipes at once instead of one at a time. This paper shows that learning multiple manipulation skills together makes the robot better at each individual skill, even with fewer practice attempts.
a-careful-examination-of-large-behavior-.industry: This paper provides a method for evaluating robot foundation models using blinded randomized trials instead of cherry-picked demo videos, which is a more rigorous standard for deployment. It shows that multitask pretraining with Diffusion Policy can improve data efficiency and robustness, which is valuable for companies deploying dexterous manipulation in logistics or manufacturing. Toyota Research Institute's approach offers a concrete way to compare robot models fairly.
a-careful-examination-of-large-behavior-.graphicPrompt: A robotic hand with multiple fingers picking up a small cube. Behind it, a grid of similar cubes in various colors. The hand is in the center, performing the task while a large circular spotlight illuminates it, with dimmer spotlights on other cubes, suggesting focus on one skill while others are learned in parallel.

diffusion-policy-visuomotor-policy-learn.tldr: Represents a visuomotor policy as a denoising diffusion process over action sequences conditioned on observations, handling multimodal demonstrations and high-frequency control.
diffusion-policy-visuomotor-policy-learn.whatChanged: Before, robot policies often struggled with multimodal action distributions and required careful smoothing or separate networks. Diffusion policy treats action generation as iterative denoising, naturally capturing multimodality and enabling stable high-frequency control. It became a default approach for imitation learning in robotics.
diffusion-policy-visuomotor-policy-learn.soWhat: Imagine a robot learning to pour milk by watching many different ways. Diffusion policy lets the robot choose the right way for each situation, like a chef picking from many recipes, by gradually refining a messy guess into a smooth, precise action.
diffusion-policy-visuomotor-policy-learn.industry: This paper became a default algorithm in commercial manipulation stacks and open-source robot learning libraries like Robosuite. It is widely used for training robots from demonstration data in research and early deployments, especially for dexterous manipulation tasks, and many follow-up works build on it as a backbone.
diffusion-policy-visuomotor-policy-learn.graphicPrompt: A robot arm reaching toward a table with scattered objects. Above the arm, a sequence of blurry action ghosts (posed hands) progressively sharpens into a clear final grip on a cube, showing denoising steps.

dreamitate-real-world-visuomotor-policy-.tldr: Fine-tunes video diffusion on human demos, uses generated video to control robot in new scenes, bridging human-robot gap.
dreamitate-real-world-visuomotor-policy-.whatChanged: Before this paper, visuomotor policies required many demonstrations per task and scene, with limited generalization. This paper shows that a single human demonstration can condition a fine-tuned video diffusion model to generate a robot execution video for a novel scene, and the robot can execute by tracking that generated video, dramatically reducing the number of demos needed and enabling zero-shot deployment in new environments.
dreamitate-real-world-visuomotor-policy-.soWhat: Instead of programming a robot or showing it thousands of examples, you can show it a video of a human doing a task once. The robot then imagines a video of itself doing that same task in a new place, and follows that imaginary video to actually do it—like watching a chef, then imagining yourself cooking in your own kitchen, then following that imagination step by step.
dreamitate-real-world-visuomotor-policy-.industry: This paper contributed a method that turns internet-scale video generators into policy engines, cutting the demonstrations needed to deploy a known task in a new environment. It suggests a path toward generalist robot skill learning with minimal data collection, relevant for manufacturing and home robotics. Toyota Research Institute may use this to accelerate robotic deployment in unstructured settings.
dreamitate-real-world-visuomotor-policy-.graphicPrompt: Left: a human hand pouring liquid from a bottle into a clear cup. Right: a robot arm and identical cup. Between them, a glowing video frame shows the robot arm performing the same pouring motion. No text or logos.

openvla-an-open-source-vision-language-a.tldr: OpenVLA is a 7B open-weight vision-language-action model trained on 970k robot episodes, enabling fine-tuning for new tasks with modest compute.
openvla-an-open-source-vision-language-a.whatChanged: Before OpenVLA, powerful robot foundation models were proprietary and required extensive resources. This paper introduced an open 7B model trained on a large multi-embodiment dataset, making fine-tuning feasible on consumer GPUs.
openvla-an-open-source-vision-language-a.soWhat: Think of OpenVLA as a robot 'brain' that can learn to control many different robots by watching lots of examples. Before, each robot needed its own custom program; now you can download a general brain and teach it new skills with just a few demos on a gaming computer.
openvla-an-open-source-vision-language-a.industry: The model provides an inspectable alternative to closed-source robot models, accelerating research and prototyping. It contributes a pre-trained checkpoint and fine-tuning pipeline using the Open X-Embodiment dataset, enabling startups and labs to build specialized robotic systems without massive budgets.
openvla-an-open-source-vision-language-a.graphicPrompt: A robotic arm reaching for a red block on a table while a glowing network diagram above shows a camera feeding images and text instructions into a brain-like cluster of nodes. Another arm on the side is connected to a consumer GPU with a wrench symbol, indicating fine-tuning.

learning-fine-grained-bimanual-manipulat.tldr: Presents ALOHA, a low-cost bimanual teleoperation rig and ACT algorithm for learning fine-grained bimanual manipulation tasks.
learning-fine-grained-bimanual-manipulat.whatChanged: Before this paper, fine-grained bimanual manipulation required expensive industrial robot arms (over $100k). The paper introduced ALOHA, an open-source, low-cost system (under $20k), and ACT, a transformer-based algorithm that learns precise actions from limited demonstrations, making high-quality bimanual data collection accessible.
learning-fine-grained-bimanual-manipulat.soWhat: This paper shows how to teach two robot arms to do delicate tasks like threading a needle or opening a tricky container using cheap parts and a smart AI method. It's like teaching a friend to cook by letting them watch your hands and practice the same movements.
learning-fine-grained-bimanual-manipulat.industry: The ALOHA hardware design and ACT algorithm became a widely copied baseline for bimanual manipulation research. Startups and academic labs adopted the platform for data collection and policy learning, reducing hardware costs from over $100,000 to under $20,000. The system has been used in subsequent works for tasks like folding clothes and assembling parts.
learning-fine-grained-bimanual-manipulat.graphicPrompt: Two low-cost robot arms with grippers teleoperated by a human holding two joystick-like controllers. The arms perform a threading task: one arm holds a needle, the other holds a thread. A camera on a tripod observes. Background shows a simple workspace with a box of tools.

bridgedata-v2-a-dataset-for-robot-learni.tldr: Introduces BridgeData V2, an open dataset of 60k multi-task manipulation trajectories across diverse environments for scalable robot learning.
bridgedata-v2-a-dataset-for-robot-learni.whatChanged: Before BridgeData V2, robot learning datasets were often limited in scale, task variety, or environment diversity, hindering generalization. This dataset provided a large, standardized collection of 60k trajectories spanning kitchens, toys, and sinks, enabling pretraining of generalist policies and systematic benchmarking of manipulation algorithms.
bridgedata-v2-a-dataset-for-robot-learni.soWhat: Think of it as a giant cookbook with hundreds of different recipes, kitchens, and utensils. A robot can practice from this book and learn to cook in any kitchen, not just one, because it has seen so many variations.
bridgedata-v2-a-dataset-for-robot-learni.industry: BridgeData V2 became one of the most widely used open datasets for pretraining robot manipulation policies, adopted by academic labs and robotics startups. It enabled more robust generalization without requiring new data collection for each task, and set a benchmark for evaluating cross-environment transfer in manipulation.
bridgedata-v2-a-dataset-for-robot-learni.graphicPrompt: A robotic arm reaching into a cluttered kitchen sink with dishes, a toy bear on a counter, and a fruit bowl on a table; the gripper open over a mug; multiple cameras and varied backgrounds suggesting different environments.

dexteritygen-foundation-controller-for-u.tldr: Pretrains dexterous motion primitives via sim-to-real RL, distills into foundation controller, uses human teleoperation as coarse prompt, improving hold stability 10-100x and enabling pen/syringe/screwdriver use.
dexteritygen-foundation-controller-for-u.whatChanged: Previously, dexterous manipulation required task-specific policies or dense human teleoperation. This paper introduces a single foundation controller that generalizes across tasks and objects, enabling long-duration in-hand manipulation and complex tool use with minimal human input.
dexteritygen-foundation-controller-for-u.soWhat: Instead of programming every finger movement, the robot learns a broad set of hand skills in simulation. A human only needs to give a rough motion hint, and the robot fills in the precise finger actions, like a dancer following a vague direction to improvise the details.
dexteritygen-foundation-controller-for-u.industry: This work contributes a pretrained foundation controller deployable on physical robot hands for assembly, lab, and service tasks requiring tool use. It reduces per-task engineering effort, allowing vendors to quickly enable long-duration in-hand manipulation and robust handling of objects like pens and syringes.
dexteritygen-foundation-controller-for-u.graphicPrompt: A robot hand holding a pen mid-air, fingers precisely rotating it. On one side, a blurred human hand making a coarse gesture. In the background, a faint grid and simulated objects fade in. No text, faces, or letters.

learning-high-speed-flight-in-the-wild.tldr: Trains a neural network to fly a quadrotor at high speed through forest trails using only onboard vision and no pre-built map.
learning-high-speed-flight-in-the-wild.whatChanged: Before this paper, high-speed autonomous flight in cluttered outdoor environments relied on motion-capture systems or pre-built maps. The paper demonstrated that an end-to-end learned policy from raw images can achieve similar performance, enabling drones to fly through unknown, unstructured terrain without external infrastructure.
learning-high-speed-flight-in-the-wild.soWhat: Think of a drone that learns to fly through a dense forest like a bird, using only its eyes and brain, instead of needing a detailed map of the forest's trees beforehand. This makes drones much more capable of navigating new places quickly and safely.
learning-high-speed-flight-in-the-wild.industry: This paper popularized vision-based end-to-end learning for drone autonomy, leading to its adoption in commercial inspection drones and autonomous systems for defense. The open-source release of code and trained models allowed startups and researchers to build custom navigation systems without expensive hardware, and companies like Skydio incorporated similar approaches into their products.
learning-high-speed-flight-in-the-wild.graphicPrompt: A quadrotor drone flying through a dense forest with tree trunks and branches on both sides; a camera mounted on the drone's front captures the scene; arrows from the camera to the onboard computer represent real-time processing; the drone's trajectory is shown as a curving dashed line weaving between obstacles.

learning-robust-autonomous-navigation-an.tldr: Learns robust autonomous navigation and locomotion for wheeled-legged robots using onboard vision and proprioception.
learning-robust-autonomous-navigation-an.whatChanged: Before, wheeled-legged robots relied on separate, manually tuned controllers for navigation and locomotion, limiting their autonomy in complex terrain. This paper introduces a single end-to-end learned policy that jointly handles both tasks using only onboard sensors, enabling autonomous traversal of stairs, ramps, rubble, and urban environments.
learning-robust-autonomous-navigation-an.soWhat: Imagine a robot with wheels and legs that previously needed a separate driver and mover; now it learns to see and move as one skill, like a person who can plan a forest path and walk it without thinking. This makes wheeled-legged robots much more capable of handling messy real-world places without human help.
learning-robust-autonomous-navigation-an.industry: This paper contributes a learning framework that integrates vision and proprioception for wheeled-legged robots, making them viable for last-mile delivery, industrial inspection, and disaster response. It shows autonomous traversal of challenging terrain without external infrastructure, providing a scalable approach for companies like ANYbotics to deploy hybrid robots in unstructured environments.
learning-robust-autonomous-navigation-an.graphicPrompt: A wheeled-legged robot ascending a rubble pile, one leg raised, wheels half-retracted. In the background, a staircase and a ramp. An inset shows a first-person camera view with a trajectory path and depth cues. No text, letters, logos, or human faces.

learning-quadrotor-control-from-visual-f.tldr: Trains quadrotor recovery policies via differentiable simulation, learning from visual features in minutes.
learning-quadrotor-control-from-visual-f.whatChanged: Before, quadrotor control training relied on reinforcement learning with millions of samples or hand-tuned controllers. This paper introduces differentiable simulation for quadrotors, enabling gradient-based optimization directly from visual features, reducing training to seconds (state) or minutes (vision).
learning-quadrotor-control-from-visual-f.soWhat: A drone can now learn to recover from a flip by 'feeling' the gradient of each action, rather than crashing thousands of times. It's like learning to ride a bike by instantly knowing which way to lean after each wobble.
learning-quadrotor-control-from-visual-f.industry: This enables drone developers to train robust recovery policies orders of magnitude faster, cutting simulation costs. Companies building autonomous drones for inspection, delivery, or cinematography can now deploy vision-based controllers with minimal trial and error. The method is directly applicable to other real-time control products requiring sample-efficient learning.
learning-quadrotor-control-from-visual-f.graphicPrompt: A small quadrotor drone in a stylized 3D simulation environment. A red arrow shows gradient backpropagation path from the drone's camera visual features through the simulator to the control outputs. The drone recovers from an upside-down position, with fading trajectory lines of previous failed attempts.

dream-to-fly-model-based-reinforcement-l.tldr: Applies DreamerV3 model-based RL to learn vision-based drone racing policies from pixels, reaching 9 m/s on real hardware with emergent gate-tracking.
dream-to-fly-model-based-reinforcement-l.whatChanged: Before this paper, model-free RL methods required large amounts of real-world data or complex sim-to-real transfers for drone racing. This paper shows that model-based RL (DreamerV3) can learn directly from pixels in simulation and transfer to real flight, achieving agile speeds with learned camera orientation behavior.
dream-to-fly-model-based-reinforcement-l.soWhat: Drones usually need explicit programming or tons of real-world practice to learn to race. This paper shows a drone can learn to fly fast by first dreaming about flying in a simulator, then waking up and doing it for real, even steering its camera to look at gates automatically.
dream-to-fly-model-based-reinforcement-l.industry: Contributed a practical method for learning drone racing policies with moderate compute/data, demonstrating model-based RL as a viable alternative to model-free methods for agile autonomy. Research labs and companies developing autonomous drones for inspection, delivery, or racing can use this approach to train policies efficiently in simulation before deploying on real hardware.
dream-to-fly-model-based-reinforcement-l.graphicPrompt: A drone with a camera on a gimbal flying through a gate. The drone's body is tilted, camera pointed toward the next gate. Background shows a simple racing course with gates. A thought bubble above the drone shows a simulated (dream) version of the same scene.

one-model-any-scenario-end-to-end-locomo.tldr: A vision-to-motor policy that handles walking, stairs, and obstacles without mapping or behavior switching.
one-model-any-scenario-end-to-end-locomo.whatChanged: Before, locomotion required separate controllers or explicit mapping and planning for each terrain type. This paper shows a single hierarchical policy can generalize across diverse scenarios directly from raw camera images and joint feedback, eliminating the need for terrain-specific software modules.
one-model-any-scenario-end-to-end-locomo.soWhat: Imagine a remote that works for your TV, stereo, and lights instead of needing a different one for each device. This paper builds a robot that uses one brain to handle flat ground, stairs, and cluttered paths without being told which is coming next.
one-model-any-scenario-end-to-end-locomo.industry: For robot vendors, this replaces multiple terrain-specific locomotion stacks with one learned model, simplifying deployment and reducing development time. Skild AI contributes this as part of their platform, enabling general-purpose robots that adapt on the fly without manual tuning or environment-specific code.
one-model-any-scenario-end-to-end-locomo.graphicPrompt: A robot with a camera on its head, a glowing neural network inside its torso directly connected to its leg motors. The camera shows three different terrains (flat ground, stairs, scattered rocks) side by side, all feeding into the same network with no separate boxes for mapping or planning.

s1-in-context-learning-for-robotics.tldr: S1 introduces in-context learning for robotics: a single video prompt specifies tasks, including unseen ones over ~10 minutes, with no weight updates and ~96% accuracy on seen tasks.
s1-in-context-learning-for-robotics.whatChanged: Before S1, robot manipulation required per-task data collection and fine-tuning. S1 removes these requirements by using in-context learning from one video prompt, enabling zero-shot execution of new tasks including long-horizon maneuvers up to 10 minutes without weight updates. It is already deployed with commercial partners, streamlining robot deployment.
s1-in-context-learning-for-robotics.soWhat: Instead of teaching a robot a new chore by showing it millions of examples and retraining it, you just show it a video once and it can copy you, even for jobs that last ten minutes. This means robots can learn new tasks on the fly, just from watching a short clip.
s1-in-context-learning-for-robotics.industry: S1 contributes a manipulation foundation model that eliminates per-task data collection and fine-tuning, reducing deployment cost and time. It provides a single video prompting interface for robot task specification and is already used by commercial partners for real-world applications.
s1-in-context-learning-for-robotics.graphicPrompt: A single robot arm with a gripper stands before a table with a cup and a bottle. A smartphone on the table displays a video of a hand pouring from bottle to cup. The robot's gripper is reaching toward the cup, indicating it has learned the task from the video.

learning-by-watching-human-videos.tldr: Finetunes omni-bodied robot model on human videos and minimal robot data to acquire new skills, bypassing teleoperation's diversity and scale limits.
learning-by-watching-human-videos.whatChanged: Before, robot skill acquisition relied on large amounts of teleoperated data, which was costly and limited in diversity and scale. This paper shows that finetuning a base model on human video with less than an hour of robot data can teach new skills, leveraging abundant internet human videos.
learning-by-watching-human-videos.soWhat: Imagine a robot that learns to cook by watching YouTube cooking shows, not by someone moving its arms for hours. This lets robots learn many skills quickly from videos people already make.
learning-by-watching-human-videos.industry: This paper contributes a method to reduce the need for expensive teleoperation data collection, enabling robots to learn from online human videos. It accelerates skill acquisition for consumer and industrial robots, and Skild AI's omni-bodied model can be used by robotics companies to quickly add new skills without extensive human demonstration.
learning-by-watching-human-videos.graphicPrompt: A large monitor displays a human hands assembling a bookshelf from an instructional video. A robot arm below the monitor reaches towards a pile of boards. Minimalist lab setting, robot arm matching the hand pose shown on screen.

learning-agile-quadrotor-flight-in-the-r.tldr: Adaptive temporal scaling and online residual learning achieve 7.3 m/s agile quadrotor flight in 100 seconds.
learning-agile-quadrotor-flight-in-the-r.whatChanged: Previously, agile quadrotor flight required precise system identification or extensive sim-to-real transfer. This paper removes those needs by using adaptive temporal scaling to explore the platform's physical limits and online residual learning with in-flight policy updates, raising speed from 1.9 m/s to 7.3 m/s in about 100 seconds.
learning-agile-quadrotor-flight-in-the-r.soWhat: Imagine learning to ride a bike by starting slowly and gradually pedaling faster, adjusting your balance in real time—no need for a perfect manual first. This lets drones learn to fly faster and more aggressively just by practicing in the real world, without expensive simulation or calibration.
learning-agile-quadrotor-flight-in-the-r.industry: The paper replaces fragile system identification pipelines with in-flight adaptation, enabling drone vendors to continuously improve aggressive flight performance after deployment. This contributes a practical, deployment-ready method for real-world reinforcement learning on physical quadrotors, directly usable by robotics and drone companies.
learning-agile-quadrotor-flight-in-the-r.graphicPrompt: A quadrotor drone with a clock gear icon on its side flies left to right. Below it, a number line with tick marks labeled 1.9 increasing to 7.3. A dashed arrow labeled 'residual' adjusts the drone's trajectory mid-flight, while a second arrow labeled 'temporal scaling' stretches the path between waypoints.

project-go-big-internet-scale-humanoid-p.tldr: Collects 100K+ home human egocentric videos; zero-shot transfers human navigation to humanoid robot without demos.
project-go-big-internet-scale-humanoid-p.whatChanged: Before, humanoid robots required robot-specific demonstrations for learning navigation. This paper shows that internet-scale human egocentric video, collected via residential partnerships, enables zero-shot transfer of language-driven navigation to a humanoid, completely bypassing robot data collection.
project-go-big-internet-scale-humanoid-p.soWhat: Imagine teaching a robot to navigate your house by watching thousands of people walk through their own homes on camera. This project makes that robot instantly able to move through a new home it has never seen, just by being told where to go in plain English.
project-go-big-internet-scale-humanoid-p.industry: Figure AI's partnership with Brookfield provides an unprecedented real-home dataset covering over 100,000 residential units, establishing a new data strategy for humanoid pretraining. This zero-shot transfer capability could dramatically reduce the cost and time of deploying humanoid robots in real-world settings like homes and commercial facilities, enabling faster iteration from simulation to physical deployment.
project-go-big-internet-scale-humanoid-p.graphicPrompt: A humanoid robot standing in a modern living room. From above, dozens of first-person video cameras stream a montage of different people walking through various home interiors. Dashed lines connect those human paths directly to the robot's legs, showing imitation without robot demos. No text, no faces.

scaling-helix-a-new-state-of-the-art-in-.tldr: Adds vision memory, state history, and force feedback, scaling demos from 10 to 60 hours for 4.05s/package at 95% barcode success on live conveyor.
scaling-helix-a-new-state-of-the-art-in-.whatChanged: Before, humanoid manipulation for logistics relied on fewer demonstrations and lacked integrated memory of past states or force feedback, resulting in slower, less reliable operation. This paper scaled demonstrations tenfold and added vision memory, state history, and force feedback, achieving near-human speed (4.05 s/package) and 95% barcode-scan success in a real distribution centre, a step toward practical deployment.
scaling-helix-a-new-state-of-the-art-in-.soWhat: Imagine a robot that learns to pack boxes by watching a human for a full work week instead of just one day. This robot can now handle bags and envelopes almost as fast as a person, and scans barcodes correctly 19 out of 20 times, making it useful for real warehouse jobs.
scaling-helix-a-new-state-of-the-art-in-.industry: This paper provides a concrete benchmark of humanoid manipulation against human speed and reliability inside a genuine distribution centre, giving logistics buyers the evidence needed to consider fleet orders. It scales the demonstration dataset from 10 to 60 hours and integrates force feedback and state history, which are critical for robust barcode scanning and package handling in cluttered conveyor settings.
scaling-helix-a-new-state-of-the-art-in-.graphicPrompt: A humanoid robot stands at a conveyor belt, gripping a poly bag envelope with one hand while aiming a barcode scanner at the bag's surface. The hand has visible force sensors. Packages and envelopes queue on the belt; a sorting chute is beside the robot. Racks of boxes line the background.

helix-a-vision-language-action-model-for.tldr: A single VLA controls a humanoid's upper body from pixels via dual-rate system on onboard hardware.
helix-a-vision-language-action-model-for.whatChanged: Previously, humanoid control either required high-end compute or separated reasoning from motor reflexes. Helix shows a single model running onboard on consumer-grade hardware, achieving fast visuomotor reflexes alongside slower reasoning, enabling generalist control in commercial pilots.
helix-a-vision-language-action-model-for.soWhat: Helix lets a humanoid robot handle both fast reflexes (like dodging a thrown object) and careful reasoning (like opening a door) using one system that runs on a regular computer. This means humanoid robots can work in real-world homes and factories without expensive, bulky hardware.
helix-a-vision-language-action-model-for.industry: Helix is deployed in commercial pilots by Figure AI, demonstrating that generalist humanoid control is feasible on consumer-grade onboard compute. This reduces cost and power requirements, accelerating potential adoption in logistics, manufacturing, and household assistance.
helix-a-vision-language-action-model-for.graphicPrompt: A humanoid robot torso at a table. A beam from its head camera hits a small onboard computer on its back. Two arrows emerge: one fast to an arm catching a ball, one slow to a hand reaching for a cup. Background shelves and household items.

introducing-helix-02-full-body-autonomy.tldr: Helix 02 replaces hand-coded full-body control with a learned neural system for continuous multi-minute real-world tasks like loading a dishwasher.
introducing-helix-02-full-body-autonomy.whatChanged: Before, full-body control for humanoid robots required 109,504 lines of hand-engineered C++ code for balancing, walking, and manipulation. This paper introduces a learned System 0 controller trained on over 1,000 hours of human motion, enabling continuous 4-minute, 61-action tasks without resets, and adds tactile and palm-camera dexterity for fine manipulation such as single-pill extraction and syringe dosing.
introducing-helix-02-full-body-autonomy.soWhat: Think of a robot that used to need a separate playbook for every muscle—now it learns a dance by watching human videos, so it can walk, balance, and handle objects smoothly at the same time. This means it can do real chores like loading a dishwasher from start to finish without stopping and without someone writing instructions for every step.
introducing-helix-02-full-body-autonomy.industry: This paper replaced massive hand-engineered C++ code with a learned neural prior for whole-body control, dramatically reducing engineering effort for deployment. It also demonstrated tactile sensing and palm cameras for precision manipulation (e.g., pill extraction, syringe dosing) on a real-world 4-minute dishwasher task. Figure AI likely uses this to deploy its humanoid robots in home or warehouse settings, and the 1,000+ hour human motion dataset provides a training resource for the field.
introducing-helix-02-full-body-autonomy.graphicPrompt: A humanoid robot at a kitchen counter, loading plates into a dishwasher. Its hands have textured tactile grips and small palm cameras. The robot walks smoothly while holding a plate, one foot stepping forward. Dishwasher door open to right, plates stacked on counter left. No faces or logos.

1x-world-model-evaluating-bits-not-atoms.tldr: Trains a video world model on humanoid data to evaluate policies in simulation, predicting real-world task success without hardware.
1x-world-model-evaluating-bits-not-atoms.whatChanged: Before, evaluating humanoid policies required expensive and risky physical hardware runs. This paper shows that a learned world model can accurately predict real-world task success from video generation, enabling screening of rare and hazardous situations without risking hardware.
1x-world-model-evaluating-bits-not-atoms.soWhat: World models let engineers test robot actions in a video simulation before trying them on a real robot, like testing a stunt in a video game before performing it in real life. This cuts the cost and danger of physical trials.
1x-world-model-evaluating-bits-not-atoms.industry: This paper contributed a method for evaluating humanoid policies using a generative video world model, reducing the time and cost of physical evaluation. Robotics companies deploying humanoid platforms can now safely test edge cases and rare events without endangering hardware. The dataset and model are built from 1X's own humanoid teleoperation data.
1x-world-model-evaluating-bits-not-atoms.graphicPrompt: A humanoid robot in a gray lab, its right side fading into a digital wireframe grid. Reaching toward a fragile vase, the real half stops short while the digital half continues, showing the vase safe in simulation.

vectornet-encoding-hd-maps-and-agent-dyn.tldr: Replaces raster HD maps with vectorized graph nodes for efficient agent trajectory prediction.
vectornet-encoding-hd-maps-and-agent-dyn.whatChanged: Before, motion prediction used rasterized bird's-eye view image stacks, which were compute-intensive and lost geometric precision. VectorNet introduced encoding HD map elements and agent trajectories as vectorized polylines and points, processed by a graph neural network, enabling direct geometric reasoning with lower compute and improved accuracy.
vectornet-encoding-hd-maps-and-agent-dyn.soWhat: Instead of drawing the road as a heavy pixel image, you draw it as connected lines and points like a wireframe. This makes it faster and easier for a computer to figure out where cars and people will go next.
vectornet-encoding-hd-maps-and-agent-dyn.industry: VectorNet became a standard representation in autonomous driving trajectory prediction stacks, cutting compute while improving prediction accuracy. It influenced subsequent models like LaneGCN and HDMapNet, and is used by Waymo and other AV companies for efficient fusion of map and agent data.
vectornet-encoding-hd-maps-and-agent-dyn.graphicPrompt: A bird's-eye view of a road intersection with connected polylines for lanes and road edges. Small directional arrows representing agent trajectories connect to nodes along the polylines, forming a sparse graph. No pixel grid, no text, no faces, no logos.

enter-the-mind-palace-long-term-active-e.tldr: Defines long-term active embodied QA with scene-graph memory and value-of-information stopping for autonomous recall, explore, or answer decisions.
enter-the-mind-palace-long-term-active-e.whatChanged: Prior embodied QA systems operated in short sessions with no persistent memory, forcing agents to re-explore environments. This paper introduces long-term memory (a scene-graph 'mind palace') and a value-of-information policy that lets the agent decide when to recall past observations, explore new areas, or directly answer a question across days or weeks.
enter-the-mind-palace-long-term-active-e.soWhat: Imagine a detective who can build a mental map of a building over several days, then when asked a question decide: do I remember the answer from before, do I need to search a new room, or can I answer now? This paper gives robots that same ability to gather information over long periods and intelligently choose what to do next.
enter-the-mind-palace-long-term-active-e.industry: This paper provides a memory architecture and decision policy that can be integrated into inspection and patrol robots for industrial facilities, enabling them to answer questions about changes over days or weeks without constant human guidance. It contributes a formal definition of the task, a benchmark environment, and a method that balances exploration and memory retrieval—directly useful for autonomous facility monitoring and security robots.
enter-the-mind-palace-long-term-active-e.graphicPrompt: A 3D scene graph hovering above a robotic wheeled platform in a warehouse aisle; the graph has nodes for objects with 'Recall', 'Explore', and 'Answer' arrows. The robot's camera is turned toward a partially opened door, with a glowing question mark above it.

intellect-2-globally-distributed-reinfor.tldr: Trains a 32B reasoning model with reinforcement learning across globally distributed, permissionless compute.
intellect-2-globally-distributed-reinfor.whatChanged: Before, large-scale RL training required centralized clusters. This paper shows it's feasible to train a 32B model using decentralized, volunteer compute with open tooling, reducing barriers for distributed training.
intellect-2-globally-distributed-reinfor.soWhat: Imagine training a robot AI using many home computers instead of one giant supercomputer. This paper showed that scattered computers worldwide can work together to teach a very large AI model, making powerful AI training more accessible.
intellect-2-globally-distributed-reinfor.industry: Contributed open communication and training tooling for distributed RL. This enables teams with scattered compute resources, like robotics startups, to train large models without owning a massive cluster. The tooling could lower costs and increase access to large-scale training.
intellect-2-globally-distributed-reinfor.graphicPrompt: A world map with small computer icons distributed across continents, connected by glowing lines, converging towards a central brain-like node labeled '32B model'. No text, no logos, no faces.

lerobot-an-open-source-library-for-end-t.tldr: An open-source library covering the full robot learning pipeline: motor middleware, dataset collection/streaming, imitation/RL algorithms, and inference on accessible hardware.
lerobot-an-open-source-library-for-end-t.whatChanged: Previously, robot learning required proprietary pipelines and expensive hardware, limiting accessibility. LeRobot provides a standardized open library that unifies the entire stack, enabling implementation on affordable robots. This democratizes development for startups and industrial users.
lerobot-an-open-source-library-for-end-t.soWhat: LeRobot is like a complete toolkit that lets you build and train your own robot assistants using off-the-shelf parts, similar to how open-source software frameworks made smartphone app development accessible to everyone. Researchers and hobbyists can now focus on teaching robots new skills instead of building the underlying infrastructure from scratch.
lerobot-an-open-source-library-for-end-t.industry: The library provides a unified platform for dataset collection and algorithm implementation, enabling rapid prototyping of robot skills on low-cost hardware. It includes standard benchmarks and pretrained models, reducing development time for startups and manufacturing facilities. Industrial users can deploy manipulation and navigation tasks on affordable robot arms and mobile bases without proprietary pipelines.
lerobot-an-open-source-library-for-end-t.graphicPrompt: A modular robot arm on a lab bench picks up a red block. A camera above streams images to a small computer running a neural network. Lines show data flowing from the camera to a database, then to a control box that sends signals to the arm's motors. No humans, no text, no logos.

neo-s-hands-an-api-to-the-physical-world.tldr: A 25-DoF tendon-driven hand with force transparency, tactile skin, and reflex robustness for the NEO humanoid.
neo-s-hands-an-api-to-the-physical-world.whatChanged: Before this paper, robotic hands typically lacked integrated force sensing, tactile feedback, and a mass-production design. This hand provides an API-like interface with high sensor density and robustness, enabling third-party developers to build applications on a standardized, widely available hardware platform.
neo-s-hands-an-api-to-the-physical-world.soWhat: Imagine a hand that can feel the weight of an egg and adjust its grip instantly without crushing it—this hand does that. It gives robots a sense of touch and precise control, turning the hand into a tool that any robot programmer can use like a smartphone's touchscreen.
neo-s-hands-an-api-to-the-physical-world.industry: This paper describes a mass-producible hand platform with 10,000 units planned for the year, serving as the physical API for the NEO humanoid. It provides industry-standard force and tactile sensing, enabling reliable manipulation tasks in home and service robotics, and is used by 1X and potentially third-party developers.
neo-s-hands-an-api-to-the-physical-world.graphicPrompt: A close-up of a robotic hand made of transparent plastic, with visible tendons and sensors inside, holding a smartphone. The palm has a glowing digital interface symbol. The arm is cutaway to show internal mechanics. No text or logos.
